findings.desc: Each loop iteration registers cleanup for `testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")`, which is the literal string `alias` rather than the IDP alias created in that iteration. findings.desc: `getForLogin` now caches realm/org login provider lists, but linking or unlinking an IDP via the organization provider only invalidates the organization caches. If a public login IDP is added to or removed from an organization after a login list has been cached, the `.idp.login.*` entries survive and continue returning the pre-link results until some unrelated IDP update invalidates them. The new test only passes because it performs an explicit IDP update before linking; direct add/remove link operations need to invalidate the login-list cache too.

findings.desc: CryptoProvider is a public SPI loaded via ServiceLoader, and adding a new abstract method means any existing third-party provider compiled against the previous interface will fail with AbstractMethodError as soon as provider detection sorts by CryptoProvider::order. Make this a default method so existing implementations remain binary/source compatible, while the built-in providers can still override their priority.
findings.title: Adding order() breaks external CryptoProvider implementations

findings.desc: DER forbids indefinite-length encodings, but readLength() returns -1 for them and readSequence() then skips the loop and returns an empty list. This causes malformed signatures to be misclassified as the wrong number of elements rather than invalid DER, and the same pattern would silently ignore indefinite-length content for any sequence. Reject negative lengths immediately in readSequence()/readNext() instead of treating them as zero content.
findings.title: DER parser accepts indefinite-length signatures as empty sequences

findings.desc: The shared KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") call does not initialize the curve, so most JDKs generate a P-256 key. The ES384 and ES512 cases then sign with SHA384withECDSA/SHA512withECDSA using a P-256 signature, while the conversion code is asked to pad it to 48 or 66 bytes. That exercises padding only, not real P-384/P-521 signatures, and can miss conversion failures around the larger coordinate sizes. Initialize the key generator per algorithm/curve instead of reusing the default EC key.
findings.title: ECDSA test uses a P-256 key for all algorithms

judgments.reasoning: The finding flags that adding an abstract order() method to the public CryptoProvider SPI can break backward/binary compatibility for external implementations and suggests making it a default method. This matches golden comment [3] about order() potentially breaking backward compatibility.

The finding flags improper handling of indefinite-length DER encodings where readLength() can return -1, leading to incorrect sequence parsing. This matches golden comment [2], which notes that starting with length = -1 causes unexpected arithmetic/processing of encoded data.

The finding points out a real test-quality issue: using an uninitialized EC KeyPairGenerator typically yields a P-256 key, so ES384/ES512 tests may not exercise true P-384/P-521 signatures and could miss conversion bugs. findings.desc: `canManage()` now grants realm-wide client management from the `Clients/manage` permission, but `canView()` only checks the legacy view roles and the `Clients/view` permission. V1 and the per-client path both treat manage as including view, and user V2 checks both VIEW and MANAGE for the analogous all-users case.
